### IV.5 Possibility of Bondi-Hoyle-Lyttleton Accretion onto the Circumbinary Disk of Source I

As summarized by Edgar [12], the Bondi-Hoyle-Lyttleton (BHL) accretion model describes a possible process of for accretion onto a moving point mass passing through a uniform gas cloud. In essence, the gravity of the mass lenses the medium into a trail in its wake. From this dense, aligned column, the mass can accrete. This model neglects pressure and thermal effects, such as the trapping of thermal energy in the trailing column. Accretion onto the disk from the ambient cloud would be limited to roughly the BHL rate, which for $n_{H_{2}}=1.6\times 10^{5}\;\text{cm}^{-3}$ , $\rho\sim 5\times 10^{-19}\;\text{g}\;\text{cm}^{-3}$ , $M=15\;M_{\odot}$ , and $v=10\;\text{km}\;\text{s}^{-1}$ . relative to the interstellar background is given by

$$ \dot{M}=\lambda_{*}4\pi\rho\frac{\left(GM\right)^{2}}{\left(v^{2}+c_{s}^{2}\right)^{3/2}}\approx 5\times 10^{-7}M_{\odot}\;\text{yr}^{-1} $$

where $c_{s}=\sqrt{k_{B}T/\mu m_{p}}$ is the ambient thermal (sound) speed $\sim$ $1\text{-}5\;\text{km}\;\text{s}^{-1}$ for $T=10\text{-}1000\;\text{K}$ , and $\mu=2.8$ . $\lambda_{*}$ is a dimensionless constant of order unity [55].

The SO line is a possible tracer of this trailing shocked ambient medium around SrcI resulting from the BN/SrcI explosion. Bally et al. [1] observed the 219.95 GHz SO line with ALMA at 1″ resolution. Figure 17 from Wright et al. [68] shows a 30″ region image centered on SrcI. The SO is seen throughout this region with a similar filamentary structure in the SiO and CO emission.

Figure 3shows SO emission around SrcI, and the expected proper motion of SrcI in 100 years. Table 1 from Rodríguez et al. [48] gives the positions and proper motions of the runaway stars in OMC1. The proper motion vector of SrcI has a PA $=$ 152 $\pm$ 4°. It appears to be misaligned by 9 $\pm$ 4°with the SrcI disk major axis (PA $=-$ 37 $\pm$ 0.4°, as observed at 220-340 GHz) [68]. The SrcI major axis aligns with the BN proper motion (323 $\pm$ 2°) [48], within 2° . This is expected, as in the BN-SrcI interaction, material in orbit around the stars experienced a torque that align their disks with the stellar proper motion vectors [2]. The small misalignment of the SrcI disk is consistent with the hypothesis that the BN-I interaction shaped the disk rather than subsequent BHL accretion. Misalignment of the SrcI disk with its proper motion may produce the turbulent wake seen in SO emission. It is also possible that this misalignment is the product of source x and the current SrcI binary, or merger remnant, having separated after the initial SrcI disk formation and relaxation.

Since the outer radius of SrcI’s disk is smaller that the gravitational radius, $r_{G}$ $\sim GM/v_{rot}^{2}$ $\sim$ 130 AU, it is likely that most of the SrcI disk has had to re-form since the dynamic interaction $\sim$ 550 years ago from pre-existing circumstellar material. This formation process may be contributing to the current accretion (and outflow). The fall-back and resulting turbulence might contribute to shocks, and enhanced accretion from disk to star.

Figure 10shows the $215.221$ GHz SO emission with uniform weighting of the u-v data to emphasize the small scale structure with a velocity resolution of $1$ $\rm km~s^{-1}$ .

The SO line shows an envelope of emission around the disk, with a steep gradient at the SE end of the disk, and an extended tail to the NW of the disk. There are also significant emission features at 0.2 to 0.4″to the NE and SW of the disk. The emission surrounding the disk is largely red-shifted, consistent with the 0.2″resolution spectra of SrcI plotted by Plambeck & Wright [44], in which the sulfur-bearing species (CS, $\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{S}$ , SO, and $\text{SO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ ) exhibit prominent blue-shifted absorption profiles.

SO and $\text{SO}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}$ are heavily absorbed across SrcI at velocities of -8 to +4 $\rm km~s^{-1}$ [68]. This blue-shifted absorption is the reason for the domination of red-shifted emission around the disk. Since the velocity width of the absorption is comparable with the halfwidth of the SiO emission lines, it is likely that the absorbing molecules are located in the (cooler) outer layers of the SrcI outflow, rather than in unrelated foreground gas [44].

In Figure 10, the $215.221$ GHz SO $\quad v=0\quad(J=5-4)$ line shows a steep gradient at the SE end of the disk, with an extended tail to the NW of the disk. The SO suggests a bow shock from the motion of SrcI through the medium, with a turbulent wake similar to the simulations in Moeckel & Throop [38]. SO is heavily present in the region around the disk, and very roughly follows a velocity pattern around the disk. The leading (SE) side of the disk has blue-shifted SO emission, while the leeward side has red-shifted SO emission. This would be expected if SO was wrapping around the disk between the outflow lobes; about half the incoming SO would have a velocity component towards us along our line of sight to the disk, and red-shifted towards the leeward side of SrcI.

Past this region, we see a significant body of SO extending away from the disk that has a small $v_{los}$ component (indicated in green, where 0 $<$ $v_{los}$ $<$ 10 $\rm km~s^{-1}$ ). Figure 11 shows the velocity structure of the trailing plume of 215.22 GHz SO emission to the NW of the disk, using natural weighting of the uv-data to enhance the brightness sensitivity in 1 $\rm km~s^{-1}$ intervals. The RMS noise level is 9 mJy/beam (35 K) in a synthesized beam FWHM 95 $\times$ 76 mas at PA -83°.

This region may correspond to the “quasi-static” body mentioned above. Material within a radius $R_{A}=2GM/\sqrt{(}c_{s}^{2}+v^{2})$ $\sim$ 90 au for $M\sim$ 15 $M_{\odot}$ , will be accreted on a time scale $R_{A}/c_{s}$ $\sim$ 300 yr [38], where $c_{s}=\sqrt{k_{B}T/\mu m_{p}}$ is the ambient thermal (sound) speed $\sim$ 1.4 $\rm km~s^{-1}$ for T $\sim$ 500 K.

In addition, studies have shown using simulations that the radiation pressure exerted by massive protostars does not preclude accretion; mass can be delivered into the star through non-axisymmetric disks and filaments that self-shield against radiation, created by gravitational and Rayleigh-Taylor instabilities while radiation escapes through optically thin bubbles [27]. Gravitational instabilities can also lead to the formation of companion stellar objects [27].

Another difficulty of getting material to infall upon massive stars is removing the angular momentum from the accreting material. The accretion disk is a mediating structure for this process, providing a buffer between the surrounding material and the protostar. For further discussion of this topic, see Pudritz & Ray [46].

The material accretes onto the disk as it loses some angular momentum, and then more angular momentum is removed through processes such as D-winds and X-winds [56], resulting in material falling onto the protostar from the disk. These steps are time-variable and may not always occur at the same rate relative to one another. X-winds are an alternative mechanism for generating outflows from disks. According to this model, high velocity outflows come from a narrow annulus where the star magnetosphere interacts directly with the inner edge of the disk, at the co-rotation radius [56]. The hot spot observed on the inner edge of the SrcI disk [13] may result from this mechanism, or alternatively from the proximity of a binary protostar. If SrcI is a binary protostar, it is not clear how the magnetospheres of the two stars interact with each other, and with the disk.

Observations of the scattered near-infrared emission suggest that the near-infrared reflection spectrum observed in the Orion-KL region is produced close to SrcI, and similar to stellar photospheres in the range Teff $\sim$ 3500 to 4500 K [59]. The spectrum excludes SrcI being a massive protostar rotating at breakup speed. Testi et al. [59] suggest that the absorption spectrum comes a disk surrounding a $\sim$ 10 $M_{\odot}$ protostar, accreting from its disk at a high rate of a few $\times 10^{-3}$ $M_{\odot}$ /yr.

Hosokawa et al. [23] studied the evolution of massive protostars with disk accretion. They identified four evolutionary phases, including deuterium burning which may account for a significant fraction of the luminosity of SrcI at some point. However their models show that that a massive protostar bloats to a radius of several hundreds of $R_{\odot}$ with an accretion rate exceeding 10-3 $M_{\odot}$ /yr. The large radius leads to a low effective temperature consistent with that observed for SrcI. They also note that the low UV luminosity will inhibit the formation of an H II region until mass accretion onto the star deceases significantly. Assuming a stellar radius of 1 AU with color temperature 4000K, the theoretical luminosity would be,

$$ L_{tot}=4\pi R^{2}\sigma T^{4}\simeq 1.01\times 10^{4}L_{\odot} $$

Comparatively, if we assume an infall rate $5\times 10^{-3}$ M⊙ / year onto a central mass of 15 M⊙, the luminosity to be

$$ L_{tot}=\frac{GM\dot{M}}{R}\simeq 1.05\times 10^{4}L_{\odot} $$

Currently, no direct observations of infall onto SrcI have been made. The expected infall rate ( $\dot{M}$ ) is inferred from the observed outflow to range from 10-5 to 10-3 $M_{\odot}$ /yr. The $\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O}$ rotation-fitting done by Ginsburg et al. [13] favor a $\sim$ 15 $M_{\odot}$ protostar with a high accretion rate. To maintain the observed luminosity of $\sim$ 104 $L_{\odot}$ , if the accretion onto the circumbinary disk is akin to the Bondi-Hoyle rate ( $\sim$ 10-7 $M_{\odot}$ /yr) and accretion from the disk onto the star is $\sim$ 10-3 $M_{\odot}$ /yr, then the disk will be depleted on a timescale of $M_{disk}$ / $\dot{M}$ . Plambeck & Wright [44] estimated Mdisk $\sim$ 0.02 to 0.2 $M_{\odot}$ , giving a disk depletion time of 200 to 2000 yr for $\dot{M}$ $\sim$ 10-3 $M_{\odot}/yr$ .

If a higher rate of accretion onto the circum-binary disk is not occurring, then the protostar will likely deplete the disk and reach the final stage of its pre-main sequence evolution. This is a rather exciting possibility, as it would expect SrcI to become a directly visible stellar object within several centuries. However, the source would still be in the Orion A cloud for a while. To emerge into the Orion Nebula would take tens of thousands of years. If it is currently $\sim$ 0.1 pc behind the ionization front with a radial velocity (v ${}_{r})\sim 4$ $\rm km~s^{-1}$ , this would take $\sim 2.5~10^{4}$ years. Also, if $\dot{M}\sim 10^{-3}$ $M_{\odot}/yr$ , the photosphere will remain on the AU scale, and after the disk is gone, it will take a Kelvin-Helmholtz time-scale to heat up from 4,000 K to $\sim$ 40,000 K for the newborn star to begin ionizing the surroundings.

### IV.6 Evidence of a Warped Disk in Salt Emission

Salt emission has been detected in nine high-mass YSO disks so far [14, 35, 58, 15]. In SrcI, salt emission is found close to the dust layer at the surface of SrcI and maps the rotation close to the disk surface [13, 14].

A comparison of the $\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O}$ and NaCl at $\sim 50\times 30$ mas resolution is shown in Figure 12. The NaCl emission is more closely associated with the continuum disk and extends to greater radii along the disk major axis than the $\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O}$ emission. Figure 4 shows the moment 1 image–the velocity weighted intensity–of the NaCl emission. This shows a simple, linear velocity gradient (implied by the linear color gradient across the disk), which is consistent with an almost edge on thick disk. Matthews et al. [34] found that the SiO masers suggest an inclination of $\sim$ 85 $\arcdeg$ . Additionally, Ginsburg et al. [13] fitted a Keplerian rotation curve to the envelope of a position-velocity along the major axis of the SrcI disk in good agreement.

Using a linear velocity gradient combined with the observed NaCl moment 0 image, we generated model images in 2 km/s channels for comparison with the data shown in Figure 13.

This simple model agrees with the observed NaCl emission in 2 km/s channels between -10 and +20 km/s. The maximum differences between the model and the data occur at the ends of the disk where the model and the data are asymmetrically offset. We used the MIRIAD tool imdiff to fit the offset as as a function of velocity. The offsets can be minimized by allowing the position angle of the disk to change with radius. A possible explanation for this disagreement at the velocity and radial extrema is that the NaCl emission resulted from (recently) accreted material having a different angular momentum compared to the original disk which resulted from the BN/SrcI encounter. Accreted material, or the localized outflow resulting from accreted material, could exert a torque. This may produce the warping observed in the 99 GHz continuum emission from the disk [69] and the NaCl emission at the ends of the disk. Alternatively, misalignment between the rotation axis and the B-field direction could also create a warped disk structure [33].

Additionally, the salt lines could be excited by infall of material onto the disk. Figure 14 shows a comparison of the 232.51 GHz NaCl $\quad v=1\quad(J=18-17)$ and the 217.98 GHz NaCl $\quad v=2\quad(J=17-16)$ in 2 $\rm km~s^{-1}$ channels. Note that the $v=1$ and $v=2$ emission come from the same regions, and have the same velocity distribution, suggesting a common origin for different transitions. This common origin may be excitation due to shocks created by accretion onto the disk.

Figure 15shows a comparison of 217.98 GHz NaCl $\quad v=2\quad(J=17-16)$ and SiO in 2 $\rm km~s^{-1}$ channels. Note that the NaCl emission that comes from the ends of the disk may be a byproduct of an accretion shock of material falling into the disk, while the SiO emerges from a smaller radius in the disk, corresponding to the footprint of a magneto-centrifugal outflow from the disk. Some of the material falling towards the disk at radii within this footprint would be swept out by the outflow.

The symmetry of the NaCl bright spots about the rotation axis may be from the rotation of the disk. If this explanation is correct, then this implies that accretion is followed by orbital redistribution i.e. the salt must stay in the gas phase for the orbital timescale at $\sim$ 30 AU radius for a 15 $M_{\odot}$ star, $>$ 40 years.

The vibrationally excited NaCl must be populated on these time scales because of the high Einstein A-values [14]. However, the density and temperature rise within 100 - 1000 yr as the shock goes through the surface layers of the disk [5]. The 1/e scale height of the disk surface estimated from the 340 GHz continuum is a only a few au [68], and presents a wide range of temperatures and densities for accreting material. More detailed modeling is needed to see if accretion shocks could populate the observed NaCl levels.

Similar to the NaCl distribution, observations of the $5_{0}-4_{0}$ (A) methanol line at 241.79143 GHz, ( $E_{u}$ 35K) in the surface layer at the ends of the disk in the Class 0 protostellar object L1157 has been previously reported as evidence for an accretion shock [64].

Ginsburg et al. [15] took a sample of 23 candidate high-mass young stellar objects (HMYSO) in 17 high-mass star-forming regions found five new detections of $\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O}$ , NaCl, KCl, PN, and SiS. While these detections had disk-like kinematic structures, SrcI is the only HMYSO that has been confirmed to have these molecules present in its disk. These results indicate that NaCl emission features are likely common in HMYSO disks.

## V Summary

1. We present ALMA observations of SiO, SiS, $\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O}$ , NaCl, and SO at $\sim$ 30 to 50 mas resolution. These images map the molecular outflow and disk of Orion Source I (SrcI) on $\sim$ 12 to 20 AU scales.

2. The SiO and $\hphantom{{}^{\text{29}}_{\text{}}}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}{}^{\mathchoice{\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$\displaystyle\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{29}$}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$\textstyle\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{29}$}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$\scriptstyle\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{29}$}}{\hbox to0.0pt{\hss$\scriptscriptstyle\vphantom{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{29}$}}}\kern 0.0pt\text{SiO}$ emission map a rotating, expanding outflow. The emission is consistent with a magneto-centrifugal outflow from the SrcI disk. The rotational velocity decreases with distance from the disk.

3. The SiS maps a turbulent boundary layer in the outflow. We argue that the SiS emission is created and destroyed in a shocked region between the outflow and the ambient medium as SrcI moves through it. This process would dissipate the angular momentum held by the rotating molecular outflow into the surrounding medium.

4. The vibrationally excited water line (Eu = 3461.9 K) traces the rotation of the SrcI disk and also traces the SiO outflow and SiS emission close to the disk, suggesting that shocks may play a role in the $\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O}$ emission. The origin of the vibrationally excited water line in the gas phase is not clear. The $\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O}$ emission extends deeper and likely formed in the disk, but icy grain mantles could not persist in the hot disk. Hydrated minerals are a possible source of $\text{H}{\vphantom{\text{X}}}_{\smash[t]{\text{2}}}\text{O}$ in the hot disk.

5. The NaCl emission closely traces the disk. The emission follows a linear velocity gradient along the disk major axis. At both ends of the disk, the position angle of the NaCl emission is consistent with a twist, or warp. Bright hot spots in NaCl emission may be excited by accretion shocks from material falling onto the disk. The motion of SrcI forces the external material to pass between the disk and the outflow, which may result in some material accreting onto the disk, creating shocks which excite the NaCl emission close to the disk surface.

6. SO traces a bow-shock at the leading edge of the SrcI disk and a turbulent plume of material extending from the trailing edge of the disk. This trailing material may accrete onto the disk. These features are created by the movement of SrcI through the medium and Bondi-Hoyle-Lyttleton accretion.

7. If the accretion onto the circum-binary disk is the Bondi-Hoyle-Lyttleton rate $\sim$ 10-7 $M_{\odot}$ /yr and accretion from the disk onto the star is $\sim$ 10-3 $M_{\odot}$ /yr to maintain the observed luminosity of $\sim$ 104 $L_{\odot}$ , then the disk is being depleted on a timescale time of 200 to 2000 yr.

8. These data suggest that the BN - SrcI interaction, and the proper motion of SrcI may have a significant effect on the structure and evolution of SrcI and its molecular outflow.

ABSTRACT 15

Host-associated bacteria must adapt to their host while also facing selection from the 16

microbiome, yet most evolution studies ignore the resident community. We experimentally 17

evolved three Pseudomonas species spanning distinct ecological roles, the foliar pathogen P. 18

syringae, the opportunist P. moraviensis, and the candidate growth-promoting P. rhodesiae, 19

through 12 passages on tomato seedlings, alone or alongside a 14-member synthetic community. 20

Relaxing competition in monoculture improved in vitro growth in two of three species, but these 21

gains did not translate uniformly in planta: monoculture-evolved P. syringae caused less disease 22

and colonized less well, polyculture-evolved P. rhodesiae colonized better across independent 23

seedling and greenhouse assays, and P. moraviensis showed no phenotypic change. Whole- 24

genome sequencing of all 36 populations identified 2,482 mutations across 101 independently 25

mutated loci. Community context reshaped the molecular basis of adaptation: monoculture drove 26

more complete selective sweeps (12.7% vs. 6.9% of mutations fixed), whereas polyculture 27

populations retained twice as much standing variation (84 vs. 42 segregating mutations per 28

population) and enriched genic mutations and hypermutator lineages in all three species. Both 29

the ecological role of a bacterium and the community context in which it evolved leave a lasting 30

imprint on evolutionary trajectories along the pathogen-to-mutualist continuum. 31

For host-associated bacteria, evolution is shaped by two potentially opposing forces: 33

selection imposed by the host and selection imposed by other members of the microbiome. A 34

colonizing lineage must adapt to the physical and immune environment of its host while also 35

navigating competition, exploitation, or facilitation from the microbes sharing that niche. 36

Because these pressures can pull in different directions, the adaptive trajectory of any one 37

lineage is difficult to anticipate from either force alone1–3. Yet most of what we know about 38

bacterial host adaptation comes from pairwise experiments conducted in the absence of the 39

resident microbiome4–6, and the few studies that do include a community show it can suppress or 40

redirect adaptation7–9, leaving unresolved whether the magnitude and direction of community- 41

mediated evolutionary change depend on a focal species’ own ecological role. The phyllosphere 42

is a tractable system for testing this: a discrete, spatially separated habitat with a resident 43

community stable enough to be defined, removed, and reconstituted experimentally10–12, where 44

synthetic communities (SynComs) have been successfully leveraged and preserve key microbial 45

interactions while retaining experimental reproducibility13. 46

Pseudomonas spans the full range of ecological roles in this habitat, from pathogen to 47

plant growth-promoting bacterium (PGPB)14, making it well suited to test whether ecological 48

role predicts evolutionary response. We evolved three species representing distinct positions on 49

this continuum: the pathogen P. syringae, the commensal P. moraviensis and the plant growth 50

promoting P. rhodesiae. P. syringae pv. tomato DC3000 is a well-characterized foliar pathogen 51

that causes bacterial speck disease and relies on a type III secretion system to suppress host 52

immunity15,16. P. rhodesiae occupies the beneficial end of the gradient, with strains acting as 53

biocontrol agents through induction of systemic resistance 17 and root architecture 54

modification18, supporting its assignment as a candidate PGPB. P. moraviensis occupies an 55


<!-- Page 5 -->


4

ambiguous position: classified as plant growth-promoting with substantial metabolic 56

versatility19,20, yet also implicated as an opportunistic, symptom-associated colonizer in diseased 57

tissue21,22. Together these species allow ecological role to be varied while host, community, and 58

evolutionary conditions are held constant. 59

We experimentally evolved all three species through 12 passages on tomato seedlings, 60

either as monocultures or alongside a constant 14-member SynCom (Figure 1 and Table 1), then 61

characterized evolved populations across in vitro growth, in planta colonization and virulence, 62

and whole-genome signatures of selection. We asked whether: (1) community presence 63

predictably shapes phenotypic evolution based on ecological role of the focal bacterium; (2) 64

microbial community presence alters the genotypic targets of selection and/or rate of molecular 65

evolution; and (3) ecological role of the focal bacterium predicts the magnitude and direction of 66

community-mediated selection. We find that while release from competition drives faster in vitro 67

growth in two of three species, these gains did not translate consistently to growth on the host 68

plant (where evolution occurred). While monoculture-evolved P. syringae lost virulence over the 69

experiment, polyculture-evolved P. rhodesiae became the strongest plant colonizer, and P. 70

moraviensis changed little on either axis. Community context also reshaped the molecular 71

landscape of all three species by lowering fixation rates, enriching genic mutations, and 72

promoting hypermutator lineages. 73

DISCUSSION 314

Integrating phenotypic and genotypic data across 36 evolved lines, we found that growth 315

improvements were species- and treatment-specific, that in vitro gains did not consistently 316

translate to enhanced in planta outcomes, that polyculture-evolved Pseudomonas increased 317

hypermutator lineages, and that parallel evolution at over 100 loci provided genome-wide 318

evidence for positive selection concentrated in largely species-specific targets. Improvements in 319

in vitro growth did not translate into elevated cell densities on seedlings in P. syringae, where 320

monoculture-evolved lines showed the greatest laboratory gains yet did not outperform ancestors 321

in planta. Rapid in vitro growth typically demands investment in biosynthetic machinery and 322

ribosome biogenesis, potentially at the expense of host-colonization traits23. The genetic basis of 323

virulence attenuation differed between the other attenuated populations: DC02 fixed a candidate 324

regulatory mutation in hdfR_2, a LysR-family regulator with known roles in flagellar and 325

virulence control24, while the other attenuated populations carried no unique fixed coding 326

mutation, pointing to polygenic low-frequency or intergenic mutations contributing to the 327

phenotype that could be explored with gene expression analyses. Adaptation to rapid growth and 328

loss of pathogenicity thus appear to be co-occurring but genetically separable outcomes of 329

monoculture evolution. 330

Across independent assays, polyculture-evolved P. rhodesiae consistently emerged as the 331

strongest colonizer, reaching higher in planta densities than the ancestor on seedlings and higher 332

Pseudomonas abundance when inoculated alone in the greenhouse, directionally corroborated by 333

rifampicin-selective CFU plating under an established community. Because a resident 334

community is a competitive barrier to colonization, this pattern is consistent with polyculture 335

passaging selecting for traits that improve establishment under interspecific competition4. These 336


<!-- Page 19 -->


18

results bear directly on the potential use of P. rhodesiae as a microbial amendment. The 337

treatment history that produced the best colonizer (polyculture) was therefore not the one that 338

produced the best host outcome (monoculture), a trade-off between colonization efficacy and 339

host cost that is directly relevant to strain selection, where both establishment and host 340

compatibility determine practical utility. 341

In contrast, P. moraviensis showed no significant phenotypic change across any growth 342

metric or in planta colonization assay, despite a mutation burden statistically indistinguishable 343

from P. rhodesiae (947 versus 959 mutations). This genomic-phenotypic discordance may reflect 344

cryptic or neutral variation buffered by genetic redundancy or epistatic compensation, well 345

documented in long-term evolution25,26. Still, the species-specific pattern of parallel evolution in 346

P. moraviensis, concentrated in transcriptional regulators, phospholipid biosynthesis, and 347

metabolic loci rather than the global regulators dominating the other two species suggest 348

adaptation along a distinct genotypic axis. 349

The mutation analysis provided strong evidence for positive selection at specific loci: the 350

nonsynonymous-to-synonymous ratio was 2.23 (monoculture) and 1.98 (polyculture), and the 351

101 genes independently mutated in three or more populations is roughly 30-fold above the 352

neutral-drift expectation. rpoB was the single most frequently mutated locus, fixed in 23 of 24 353

populations across P. moraviensis and P. rhodesiae but entirely absent in P. syringae. We 354

interpret this cautiously. All lines were passaged under continuous rifampicin selection, and rpoB 355

is the canonical target of rifampicin resistance27. P. syringae DC3000 carries innate resistance 356

through a different mechanism, whereas the P. moraviensis and P. rhodesiae ancestors were 357

themselves made rifampicin-resistant immediately before the experiment, almost certainly via an 358

initial rpoB mutation. The recurrent rpoB mutations we observe therefore likely reflect, at least 359


<!-- Page 20 -->


19

in part, continued optimization or compensation of that induced resistance under sustained 360

antibiotic selection28, rather than host- or community-driven selection alone. This does not 361

exclude a genuine adaptive role, since RNA polymerase mutations are well-documented general- 362

purpose targets in antibiotic-free evolution experiments 29, but the strength of rpoB as evidence 363

for host-associated selection specifically should be weighed against this alternative. 364

Beyond rpoB, parallel evolution converged on flhA in P. rhodesiae (12 of 12 365

populations), consistent with the well-documented loss-of-motility trajectory in which non- 366

motile variants outcompete motile ancestors by shedding the energetic cost of flagellar 367

biosynthesis, and possibly reducing chemotaxis-driven competition or phage susceptibility in the 368

community context30. BLASTx annotation of hypothetical targets (Supplementary Table S8) 369

recovered three further recurring themes: carbon and nutrient acquisition from host-derived 370

substrates; membrane and abiotic-stress adaptation in P. moraviensis; and interbacterial 371

competition, with five hypothetical loci across both commensals annotating to Rhs/T6SS toxin 372

components including DddA-family deaminases31,32. Notably, one such locus 373

(DDAHOALL_04353) appeared exclusively in polyculture-evolved lines, suggesting that 374

community context selected for competitive traits, while the other four appeared in both 375

treatments, suggesting this pressure is not confined to the polyculture environment. 376

A consistent pattern across axes was that monoculture-evolved lines showed stronger 377

signatures of adaptation, particularly phenotypically: monoculture P. syringae and P. rhodesiae 378

showed the greatest in vitro gains, monoculture populations had a higher fixation rate (12.7% 379

versus 6.9%), and hypermutator lineages were enriched in polyculture (6 of 18 versus 0 of 18; 380

Fisher’s exact p = 0.0095). The SynCom likely imposed a more variable, multidimensional 381

selective environment in which no single mutation consistently conferred an advantage, making 382


<!-- Page 21 -->


20

complete sweeps less likely33,34; community members may also have reduced focal effective 383

population size by competing for space and nutrients or increased stress35. To distinguish these 384

mechanisms, we suggest direct abundance estimates of microbial members during passaging and 385

manipulation of community diversity. 386

Ecological role along the pathogen-to-PGPB continuum influenced the direction of 387

evolutionary change. P. syringae gained in vitro growth while losing virulence through at least 388

two mutational routes; P. rhodesiae showed a community-dependent colonization advantage 389

paired with a monoculture-specific reduction in host cost; and P. moraviensis, despite a 390

comparable mutation burden, showed no detectable phenotypic change on any axis assayed. 391

Ecological role thus shapes whether and how a species responds to community membership 392

more reliably than it predicts the magnitude of that response. Community context consistently 393

shifted the molecular landscape across all three species by lowering fixation rates, enriching 394

genic mutations, and promoting hypermutators. That the same ancestor, host, and passage regime 395

produced different phenotypic outcomes depending only on whether competitors were present 396

indicates that community context leaves a durable evolutionary legacy, and that adaptation is 397

contingent not just on genetic background36 but on the ecological history of the lineage. 398

Predicting how plant-associated bacteria evolve under complex agricultural microbiomes will 399

therefore require considering ecological identity, community context, and the selective pressures 400

introduced by the experimental design itself. 401
